title: Where Earth's Water Came From
objective: After this level you can explain the leading ideas for where Earth's water came from.
summary: Deuterium is water's origin clue. Asteroid meteorites match Earth; comet 67P seemed not to, until 2024. Some water came from within Earth. The shares are debated.

cards.headline: Earth was born too hot to keep its water. Or was it?
cards.body: For a long time, scientists thought any water on the newborn Earth would have boiled off or blown away into space, so the oceans must have arrived later, on comets or icy asteroids. So who delivered the sea? The answer is still being argued over.

cards.headline: A fingerprint in every drop
cards.body: Water carries a clue. Its hydrogen comes in two kinds: ordinary hydrogen, and a rare, heavier form called deuterium. Deuterium forms more readily in cold places far from the Sun, so the share of it in water hints at where that water formed. The test is simple: find a space rock whose water has the same fingerprint as your bathtub.

items.label: Comets
points: Its water has more than three times Earth's deuterium ratio
Verdict then: comets like it are unlikely suppliers

items.label: Asteroids
points: Meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites carry water
A 2014 WHOI-led study: Earth got its water early from such bodies

cards.headline: Case reopened
cards.body: In 2024, a NASA-led team found that dust had skewed Rosetta's readings, and that 67P's water looks much like Earth's after all. A 2020 study added a twist: meteorites like the stuff Earth formed from hold enough hydrogen to supply at least three times the water in the oceans. Today's picture is a mix. Some water came from inside Earth, vented by volcanoes, and much came from asteroids and possibly comets. How much from each is still debated.

cards.headline: Water's origin: debated
learned: Some water came from inside Earth; shares still debated
